    "thumbnail": "https://i.ytimg.com/vi/48pxVdmkMIE/maxresdefault.jpg",
    "description": "Sergey Levine is one of the world’s top robotics researchers and co-founder of Physical Intelligence. He thinks we’re on the cusp of a “self-improvement flywheel” for general-purpose robots. His median estimate for when robots will be able to run households entirely autonomously? 2030.\n\nIf Sergey’s right, the world 5 years from now will be an *insanely* different place than it is today. This conversation focuses on understanding how we get there: we dive into foundation models for robotics, and how we scale both the data and the hardware necessary to enable a full-blown robotics explosion.\n\n𝐄𝐏𝐈𝐒𝐎𝐃𝐄 𝐋𝐈𝐍𝐊𝐒\n* Transcript: https://www.dwarkesh.com/p/sergey-levine\n* Apple Podcasts: https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/fully-autonomous-robots-are-much-closer-than-you-think/id1516093381?i=1000726524050\n* Spotify: https://open.spotify.com/episode/1WpOKLN3vSvvWjrVDIJAyy?si=DPxf6K5BSBy5R4OYIqk8pQ\n\n𝐒𝐏𝐎𝐍𝐒𝐎𝐑𝐒\n* Labelbox provides high-quality robotics training data across a wide range of platforms and tasks. From simple object handling to complex workflows, Labelbox can get you the data you need to scale your robotics research. Learn more at https://labelbox.com/dwarkesh\n\n* Hudson River Trading uses cutting-edge ML and terabytes of historical market data to predict future prices. I got to try my hand at this fascinating prediction problem with help from one of HRT’s senior researchers. If you’re curious about how it all works, go to https://hudson-trading.com/dwarkesh\n\n* Gemini 2.5 Flash Image (aka nano banana) isn’t just for generating fun images — it’s also a powerful tool for restoring old photos and digitizing documents. Test it yourself in the Gemini App or in Google’s AI Studio: https://ai.studio/banana\n\nTo sponsor a future episode, visit https://dwarkesh.com/advertise\n\n𝐓𝐈𝐌𝐄𝐒𝐓𝐀𝐌𝐏𝐒\n(00:00:00) – Timeline to widely deployed autonomous robots\n(00:17:25) – Why robotics will scale faster than self-driving cars\n(00:27:28) – How vision-language-action models work\n(00:45:37) – Changes needed for brainlike efficiency in robots\n(00:57:59) – Learning from simulation\n(01:09:18) – How much will robots speed up AI buildouts?\n(01:18:01) – If hardware’s the bottleneck, does China win by default?",

    {

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "It has already entered into quantum realms. It was guided to do that maybe in the last 1 year.",

    {
      "id": "Ugy6ZOlTsR0Bx5ZVFe54AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Stop asking him to predict magnitudes, after he's made it clear he hasn't thought much about it, but rather about solving the robotics problems at-hand.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC0P1bOeHMJZk9CNp-Cdd32g",
      "author": "@channel11121",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/t42Trh554qtaR9eMPggMb_RtQqyR3ItdNjsM_DM2qvah18NVs2OBwVIUlXsxrCN-VLKuen-DEw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "timestamp": 1773878400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugxprm-TB8tYxU44MSZ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Darkwesh, it's really annoying when you press these brilliant researchers on giving you a specific date on when the technology will reach x level.\n\nIt comes off as you trying to get a headline for your video, rather than truly listening to what the researcher is saying.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC8l2kFclPVkyDvyZxddZMzQ",
      "author": "@nicolasgonzalezl",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_m-DM4YsMJ-Xnl308DDAKJjMpW8lF_tgEJetivIhIfKCXBt=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "1 month ago",
      "timestamp": 1773878400,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "Ugz4klVU5pJIDRd7L4d4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The reason that the \"flywheel\" is more relevant for robotics than text, is that there is simply more high-quality textual data already out in the world, and not much physical control data, so the relative utility of such \"flywheel\" data in robotics is much higher.",
      "like_count": 0,

      "id": "UgzrNBYReHs9XznFtMp4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I call BS. Humanoids have ALWAYS been (and will be) useless as workers. \nWe see how Amazon and others are replacing people and it's not with humanoids. Because robots ALREADY use Vision and AI and they don’t look like humans because humans are limited. (they have to climb ladders, hands too big for small things etc.) Automation has been replacing people for decades and it hasn't stopped! So if a humanoid could do it, it’s already automated! (1) Just look at history. (2) So NO, they WON'T become useful as technology and AI improves.\r\n\r\nIn other words. The typical factory job is doing things that robots(automation) cannot do. And humanoids ARE robots. The form does not matter.\r\n\r\nLook at it this way. If AGI could assemble widgets or do surgery or manicures, etc. it would need special tools not batteries, hands and legs. Optimus is not strong enough to dig a hole or help someone get up off the floor. It can't even work at McDonalds. If it makes a mess putting popcorn in a cup with a human brain behind it, could it do much better with an artificial one? Can it wash its hands? How long would it take it to change gloves, start a roll of tape etc.? A humanoid MUST do a job on par with a person because workplaces are made so people along with machines maximize asset utilization. That is why you CAN'T just put two humanoids in place of one person.\r\n\r\nThis is why no one has EVER shown ANY humanoid doing any useful job that a person was paid to do. But AI could make it a fun toy or criminal.\r\n\r\nIf you have a trade job, you’d realize it would be impossible or impractically slow to do it with robot hands. Have you ever seen it use hand tools? No amount of AGI Learning or training is going to make the hands better with tools, scissors, small parts etc. Making hands equal to a person is impractical and unnecessary.\r\n\r\nHot, heavy, dirty and dangerous jobs. There are 100s of millions of them around the world. And if a humanoid could actually do it, LOL, most of those jobs pay super low wages in places where there is no electricity to charge it anyway.\r\n\r\nMost of today's humanoids can barely complete the tasks from the DARPA robot challenge 10 years ago !?!\r\n\r\n\"Optimus will be the best surgeon\" !? When AGI can do surgery, it will use existing surgical robots. A humanoid will not wield a scalpel.\r\n\r\n\"it's a humanoid so it can work in a human environment\" if it's not useful then that doesn't matter.\r\n\r\nWho will buy them? Certainly not factory or warehouse managers. They can't do trade jobs or hard labor. They will be lousy housekeepers, tour guides, popcorn servers, entertainers etc. ridiculed as toys and criminals will use them for nefarious purposes. At best it could be a checkout clerk that will restock the store at night if it ever really gets a brain. Credit only, robot hands can’t handle money well.\r\n\r\nBut they would be really nice if a handicapped person could use it as a telepresence to go shopping, do simple chores, etc. Please make a version like this.\r\n\r\n(1) It's first principles. If the goal is to emulate a human then you must make a humanoid/android. But if the goal is doing things that a human can do, then first principles DOES NOT dictate a humanoid. So AI is already \"embodied\" or \"physical\". (ill conceived terms, us old folks say, smart sensor or smart tv) And if you do want to emulate a human, you must choose which characteristics you want. It may need sensitive hands to feel slight imperfections or it may need durable hands for hard work. So a one-size-fits-all like Optimus is not practical. Unless it can reproduce, heal and recharge itself for decades by simply eating and sleeping.\r\n\r\n (2) Warehouse managers needed people to store and retrieve items. Now warehouses are full of non-humanoid smart robots. People had to pick parts out of a pile and place them with correct orientation. Now one arm one eyed robots do it. People had to pick up parts to inspect and measure them. Now lasers measure them and vision systems inspect them. PID controllers became self tuning. As tech/learning/AI improved, so did machines and machine controllers. Just like computers taking jobs with spreadsheets and scanners. All the while someone was saying a humanoid will soon do the work.",

      "text": "after 12', the youtuber asks an absurd and totally illogic thing, how many years the robots needs of learning in order to produce a large chunk of human work in terms of revenues: i can answer him rapidly: never, since in capitalism this is not a matter of productivity (the increasing of which  is the only way a human worker could hope to maintain his salary to survive and reproduce), but it is a matter of exploitation: you cannot \"exploit\" a machine, so replacing a worker with a machine can exponentially improve the productivity as a whole, but on an average cycle of a free market it would be catastrofic for profits and revenues of the capitalist",

      "text": "I didn't think I'd come away from this talk having lengthened my timeline for household robots but here we are.       "parent": "root",
      "text": "Oddly, this video actually made me lengthen my AGI timeline.       "id": "Ugyhy2u9Aneu60CKeiN4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "The brain is more like having many CPUs/threads operating at the same time on different values, rather than a GPU that has to take a static matrix of values one at a time. The brains neurones are unconstrained in their parallelism. IMO we will return to CPUs for AI, at least for the later stages of cognition (early sensory processing will be done by GPU-like ASICs, specifically for the given type of sensor, which a more abstract/high level model will then ingest and use, and most likely be run on CPUs, or neuromorphic hardware).",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCWkS5yqP6iVjqOnxdMYPB6Q",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Compared to the Bernt Børnich interview of 1x Technologies that I've seen a month ago, this interview with Sergey Levine made me really bearish on robotics. The scale seems very \"university research lab\". Børnich on the other hand mentioned things like they invented their own motors that are a gearless design with +5x nominal torque possible by current/torque controller that is neural net based. He said their robots have to be offline with the compute inside the robot to adjust fast enough and explained muscle delay in humans and how nature adjusted. He also talked about his vision for scaling up and their simulation partnership with nvidia and that later this year they will ship the first neo gamma robots to early adopter homes.",

      "author_id": "UCYkxsAbBVQmbyQ4biBds3Mw",

      "parent": "root",
      "text": "🎯 Key points for quick navigation:\n\n00:28 🤖 Physical Intelligence is focused on creating general-purpose robotic foundation models for versatile task performance.\n01:29 🧺 Current robots can perform basic tasks like folding laundry, but this is just the beginning of their capabilities.\n02:55 🗣️ Future robots should autonomously manage complex household tasks based on simple prompts and adapt over time.\n03:52 📈 Successful robots will require common sense, continuous learning, and the ability to handle edge cases intelligently.\n04:45 🔄 Once robots demonstrate basic competence, they can be deployed to learn and improve from real-world experience.\n05:40 ⏳ Expect robots to be useful in single-digit years, potentially within one to two years for basic tasks.\n07:25 🤝 Human supervision will help robots improve quickly through collaborative learning from both actions and verbal instructions.\n09:28 🛠️ The scope of robotic capabilities will gradually expand as they gain more skills, similar to the evolution of coding assistants.\n10:50 💼 In five years, robots may handle most blue-collar work, but this will depend on the scope of tasks they can perform.\n13:00 🚀 Gradual integration of robots in a human-in-the-loop setup will enhance their effectiveness and productivity.\n18:34 ⚙️ Advances in perception technology have improved robotics since the early days of     {
      "id": "Ugxs16iNUAsV1NLuzeh4AaABAg.AN-mpZOKfJCAN07sbn8r_d",
      "parent": "Ugxs16iNUAsV1NLuzeh4AaABAg",
      "text": "Also strange to give that as an example of compositional generalization. If you have a dictionary with English and IPA spellings, then you literally have a lookup table in the training data. Compositional generalization would be if you had half a dictionary, and it figures out the other half, by inferring English pronunciation rules (as far as there are such rules) and how to compose them (for example if it had seen the example knife-knives and the IPA spellings, and inferred how wife-wives should be pronounced. But it might get confused by life-lives, since there are two pronunciations of lives).\n\nThere is evidence that Transformers can learn compositional generalization, but it looks like it requires a different kind of learning task then the next-token predictions that LLMs are mainly trained to do (see \"Human-like systematic generalization through a meta-learning neural network\" )",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCkmPmJg_lilce6bRc_0Hz4Q",

      "id": "UgzpbwUr65_InGR7MzJ4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "Curious if a foundational model for robotics can really be conceived independent of the form factor. Is that even possible? And if, say, Clone Robotics wanted to use the same model, how much customization would be needed?",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCS0iwhdLxj5ObC5Dl-lzzWw",
      "author": "@CSAILearning",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_k1Xp3OrktpqNwGhtbo6zA1N8xZfM2-ivxM7ptxl7Dd_E2Ehrne9RE1y1nc08gin6WZJg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "7 months ago",

      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgzpbwUr65_InGR7MzJ4AaABAg.AN-XcewIxeaAN3I-qUc4uN",
      "parent": "UgzpbwUr65_InGR7MzJ4AaABAg",
      "text": "I'll offer a little personal experience. I'm a fairly serious hobbyist in the AI/RL and robotics space. A few weeks ago I wrapped up a course that included a small mobile robot with SLAM(think basic autonomous navigation) in a simulator. I'm three weeks into making that same functionality work in a \"mirrored\" physical robot and it's not the hardest thing I've ever worked on, but there have been some pretty significant challenges..and that's an identical robot going from sim to real. \n\nI can also say that training models for RL tasks tends to require you to know your outputs/inputs ahead of time, and even small changes can throw things off. Something trained to play chess from one side won't understand intuitively how to play from the other side like a human would. That's something you have to think about ahead of time and build into your training, or sanitize your inputs for consistency. \n\nSo, if we combine those things, I can say that applying any kind of software to the physical world is going to have hurdles, and applying a robotics AI model to something it wasn't designed for is going to be difficult. Difficult isn't the same thing as impossible though. I can see a world where we standardize on enough inputs/outputs across various bots to use shared models, assuming they allow heavy configuration. \n\nWhat I suspect we'll see more of in the near future is limited models integrated for common functionality. Maybe your robot follows a traditional algorithm to drive to the kitchen, but one model is connected to a ChatGPT API, to recognize that you asked for breakfast, and another robot arm model takes over to open the fridge and start cooking eggs. \n\n\nJust my 2c.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCq6-U1MfzA61gMAXP8CtdzA",

      "id": "UgzpbwUr65_InGR7MzJ4AaABAg.AN-XcewIxeaAN4DTuOp-kq",
      "parent": "UgzpbwUr65_InGR7MzJ4AaABAg.AN-XcewIxeaAN3I-qUc4uN",
      "text": " @robertcowher  That’s just as I suspected. Unless hardware–AI model combinations are pretrained together, it’s hard to call anything a foundational model. What I find intriguing about Physical Intelligence is that they use the term “foundational model” in a way that seems closer to how it’s applied to multipurpose LLMs. But I doubt their model would transfer seamlessly across humanoids like Figure, Optimus, or Neo—unless those robots share exactly the same configurations. Or may be I misunderstood their terminology?\n\nThat said, I agree with building reconfigurable robots from standardized subsystems, each trained on multipurpose models. For that to work, we’d also need an interoperability layer—something akin to MCP.",

      "text": "@ 23:48 Well said, \"scalable means generalizable\"\n\n@ 25:40 Interesting about \"common sense, plus the ability to make mistakes and corrections\"\n\n@ 31:10 IMHO, humanoid robotics is the hardest problem to solve.\n\n@ 31:30 That data fly wheel is likely going to be an autonomous agent in 4D simulation and then \"birthed\" into the real world.\n\n@ 31:52 Yes, Reinforcement Learning as an autonomous agent.\n\n@ 32:45 Very interesting VLM and action cortex and using diffusion.\n\n@ 34:50 Leverage of Prior Knowledge, though the question was more centered on recognition of a common core algorithm.\n\n@ 39:10 Representations.  This reminds me of the idea of telescoping discussed by a control systems professor.\n\n@ 42:18 I agree, especially when applying Reinforcement Learning with Fuzzy Logic.\n\n@ 44:45 Fascinating international phonetic alphabet (I think this is a common language, relative, geometry)\n\n@ 48:50 Moravec's Paradox \n\n@ 1:03:05 Prior Knowledge, can get it from simulation (with a lot of noise!).\n\n@ 1:04:45 I totally agree with Sergey, and I actually think he is making a big understatement, in that, the core of machine intelligence, likely originated from an epically \"simple\" robotics, Reinforcement Learning, experiment that used Fuzzy Logic, with \"the simplest robot\" as an adaptive control system that was able to focus or warp the state space to experience (described in \"Scott Kuindersma: Controlling Multi-Contact Robot Behaviors with Optimization | IACS Seminar\" video on YouTube).\n\n@ 1:05:34 This is how the potential of, the combination of, Reinforcement Learning, with Fuzzy Logic, has not only the potential to learn any relative symbolic language, but also the physics of the world, via a language action output.\n\n@ 1:08:45 Meta Learning as an emergent.  Right objective.  One key not said though is noise in simulation.\n\n@ 1:24:30 On China vs. USA, in Machine Intelligence (\"AI\").  I think China is winning this race, for the last quarter century, or more (basically an entire generation of students) because they supported their STEM students more, not just by giving them a free education and fully supporting their cost of living, but also providing free, universal healthcare.  Meanwhile, for the same time period, the United States has done the polar opposite, by burdening STEM students with high tuition debts, but also bankrupting them, if they have no health insurance, and get sick.\n\n@ 1:29:00 well said, balance of strategy on hardware.\n\n@ 1:31:45 Sergey hit the nail on this one.  STEM Education has been way undervalued in the United States (especially for non-military industrial complex jobs) for the last quarter century, or more, and this is exactly why we are now in this giant conundrum with China respecting their STEM students much more for the same generation.       "id": "Ugx9Br0wugmb0anobv14AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "My main concern about robot is that robots have a much larger fixed cost comparing to LLM for deployment. And you need to get it economically viable to actually have the flywheel running.",

      "author_id": "UCRvz2_45Padz7OZdujkOWug",
      "author": "@yizhizhu5154",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_k8ujdlFK7Pjq7q7yUv1JiTDpgik8PxiPdfCAHR5QV0NQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "Ugx9Br0wugmb0anobv14AaABAg",
      "text": "Which is why you have something like Tesla, where you can deploy for actual tasks to improve the robots for economically viable tasks, but not pay the full deployment cost (or at least mitigate it), like a customer. While I agree that it is a much larger fixed cost, the offset to any physical human task is at least as profitable as an llm in corporate savings (when it works).",

      "author_id": "UC6WwQqvUS41ikynz6THbozA",
      "author": "@charlesK001",

      "parent": "Ugx9Br0wugmb0anobv14AaABAg",
      "text": "This is why the idea of domestic robots doing house work is a distant fantasy. Products are valued at what people are willing to pay for them, and a robot capable of taking care of a household is good enough to take care of an office, work in a factory, be useful for the military. There is far more money and demand in those markets than there is in domestic housekeeping, so robots will be sold for and populate those markets first. And once robots are in the workforce, we won’t even be able to afford a home, let alone a robot to take care of it.",

      "id": "Ugw-CV-qAW6aeYIkdNp4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "12:04 You can't just use the revenue of the AI companies to determine the value LLMs are producing in the economy, because the individuals and companies that are using the LLMs are receiving value from them which is generating money (and saving money) for them, which is separate from the revenue of the AI companies themselves. For example, if a company buys access to an LLM for $1000 per year, and that allows a 10 person team to become a 5 person team by using it, and the 5 people that were let go were making $100K per year each, that resulted in the company effectively profiting $499K despite only paying $1000 for the LLM. All that value generated in the economy goes unreported if you're only looking at the $1000 payment to the AI company. On top of that there is also the value generated by the LLM's work output, for example if it's used to create a product that sells for $1M, now the company profited $1.499M just from that $1000 payment to the AI company. So in summary there's not a 1-1 ratio for the AI companys' revenue to the value LLMs are producing in the economy. Similarly to how you can't just look at an employee's paycheck to determine the value that employee generated in the economy.",
      "like_count": 9,
      "author_id": "UCy-jIjlzdpwS1TmrYjUCzZA",
      "author": "@Blakostructr",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_lJSw1MPSORrjNlKysOYiPw2ut3PgQ9KDDf-vZWsI8=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "text": "I believe the first sign that ai is impacting gdp without us noticing is that people between the age of 20-25 are staying unemployed longer. Why hire a new entry level person when all the monotonous work that needs to be done can be done by the people already in the firm.",

      "author_id": "UCLx3bCki0Ie4Km3ICHBw1Hg",
      "author": "@Luke-eo6kp",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nkzbjaGEJHUvve8VQI0YuVLVxkd8JaPc6Tx9XdAgNV_ss=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "Ugw-CV-qAW6aeYIkdNp4AaABAg",
      "text": "Incorrect, you are forgetting that the value in the economy also cannot forget about individuals.     {

      "parent": "Ugw-CV-qAW6aeYIkdNp4AaABAg",
      "text": "The market is becoming more competitive, and value for dollar is better known now. In 20 years there will be a close correlation between money spent on AI and its value.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCVzMC2zzYo8EYzuiEF_S8Ww",
      "author": "@czinn327",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/d-SmI-HmqzMW5IUbOI1AAVjdNjQCX04ZM6ZdAMfOpw_OCUKbZhHt3CchWui6jYTtNvJ377XuTQ=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "They have been saying this for fully self driving cars for decades. I will wait till I see it.",
      "like_count": 28,
      "author_id": "UC13UHBjUdUAl8wrfZyCNKyQ",
      "author": "@specials6165",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_ncxsqkK-TwVMj45JU6frURtO6J8SHEPZut4aUO1DI4Cg=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,

      "_time_text": "7 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1758240000,
      "is_pinned": false

    {
      "id": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqAN3Nu1JLoq1",
      "parent": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg",
      "text": "Full self driving is a much harder problem to solve. Compared to a robot that works in a relatively controlled environment, autonomous vehicles must solve far more situations with significantly more variables, at life and death velocities. \n\nSociety can give a robot multiple chances at putting a box on a shelf or folding a towel. But it can’t give autonomous vehicles multiple chances at running a red light or swerving into oncoming traffic.",
      "like_count": 4,
      "author_id": "UCekQYdFj3zNaR52M_04PGJw",
      "author": "@wonmoreminute",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/oYzPugPZKbf3xUeu47Z3hsY7m9h0IHLTGZc89GWyEyk-7qIlO2C_Y3ggXMOgxJe74YIVZAZ3hA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "7 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1758240000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqAN8sDA1ziBS",
      "parent": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg",
      "text": "This is why I don't trust his interview. General robots are harder than self-driving cars. I do not buy his \"well our robots do less dangerous things\" as an argument that robots will outpace self driving cars. \n\nThis entire contention sounds like CEO investor hype bullshit.",
      "like_count": 2,
      "author_id": "UCpVjFlOka1qBLvEVkeu7DAA",
      "author": "@carlemueller",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l5TF7keed3UIKtj2nP8ljY1KVleiO_l9qu3fXaURmwZQk=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "7 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1758240000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqANJxvQ1H9XP",
      "parent": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqAN8sDA1ziBS",
      "text": " @carlemueller  It's because you're not familiar with how the sausage is made.\n\nA brain is a collection of synapses. More 'intelligent' animals tend to have more of them. Almost every recent big 'breakthrough' in AI was thanks to our computer hardware getting less bad.\n\nGPT-4 was about the size of a squirrel's brain. The datacenters coming online this year with 100,000+ of the GB200 will be around human scale. Running at 2 Ghz, aka, 50 million subjective years to our one.\n\nThe hardware to drive robots and cars will not be made directly by human hands and human minds. The giant AGI datacenter is supposed to build out an NPU substrate (this is a more hard-wired neural network, instead of an abstraction. Running at animal-like speeds so as to not need 50 million times as much electricity to run than needed) to put into these things.\n\nAGI is the most valuable invention we can make, and capital is putting all it can into making it a reality. The robot army that'll replace us is more of a footnote to that, honestly.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC7RWnz65ck3XW44mArmWqRQ",
      "author": "@everythingisterrible8862",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_l4aEfh_jJF9zK20QQIgQQyFIda2bzJeFkhVjY6Xs0BwI1bV9Y4Il7Wvg0pj_SFi1Uq-A=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "6 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1760832000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },

      "text": "Self driving cars are already a thing... What are you talking about?",

      "author_id": "UC6NECm5KPF7fpPKLhi8rMow",

      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nWJbMzxyWs9GutynesnfDgvYqapmJyCr3RmMl3L1DUxA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqAN-uS1__Hg-",
      "text": " @adrianclark2734 To be fair, OP said fully self driving. We don’t yet have level 5 autonomous vehicles on our roads.",
      "like_count": 5,
      "author_id": "UCekQYdFj3zNaR52M_04PGJw",
      "author": "@wonmoreminute",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/oYzPugPZKbf3xUeu47Z3hsY7m9h0IHLTGZc89GWyEyk-7qIlO2C_Y3ggXMOgxJe74YIVZAZ3hA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqAN3Ma-L07wg",
      "parent": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqAN3LoXVNfeB",
      "text": "​ @wonmoreminute  but what we have, are for all points and purposes, fully self driving. Sure, we still have to have eyes on the road at all times, but the tech is already there, and indeed, getting better at an alarming rate through world models. As are robotics. I just think it's a bit pretentious distinction to make.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UC6NECm5KPF7fpPKLhi8rMow",
      "author": "@adrianclark2734",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/ytc/AIdro_nWJbMzxyWs9GutynesnfDgvYqapmJyCr3RmMl3L1DUxA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "7 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1758240000,

    {
      "id": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqAN3QgX_Gk3C",
      "parent": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqAN3LoXVNfeB",
      "text": " @adrianclark2734 No, it’s not pretentious. We are not even close to level 5 autonomy. We’ve exhausted the low hanging fruit, the stuff you teach your 16-year-old in their first hour of driving. \n\nIf solving vehicle autonomy was like getting into space, we’ve reached the upper limits of the atmosphere. But breaking out of the atmosphere and reaching orbital velocity requires orders of magnitude more energy. \n\nLikewise, the difference in compute requirements and capability between a vehicle that requires your eyes on the road and your hands ready at a millisecond notice, and a vehicle that you send empty to the far side of the city to pick up your eleven year old from piano lessons and bring them home safely in rush hour traffic during a snow storm is orders of magnitude greater. Pretentious is not recognizing the difference.",
      "like_count": 1,
      "author_id": "UCekQYdFj3zNaR52M_04PGJw",
      "author": "@wonmoreminute",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/oYzPugPZKbf3xUeu47Z3hsY7m9h0IHLTGZc89GWyEyk-7qIlO2C_Y3ggXMOgxJe74YIVZAZ3hA=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",
      "author_is_uploader": false,
      "author_is_verified": false,
      "is_favorited": false,
      "_time_text": "7 months ago",
      "timestamp": 1758240000,
      "is_pinned": false
    },
    {
      "id": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqAN47Ow5F8ne",
      "parent": "UgyRVTV-dyuwdIE-sQd4AaABAg.AMzKHAB0FfqAN3LoXVNfeB",
      "text": "​ @wonmoreminute  I wonder how much of it is them trying to figure out a price model before they roll out the real thing? Unless you think that we never get human level decision making for self driving cars, which I will allow can't be ruled out based on your argument that there is a very big leap between \"driving\" and \"Driving\". In your own words, we're not close, which to me means at least a decade. My prediction for the next decade is that if there are plateaus in solving for current problems, they will become extremely clear by 2035. We will have a good handle on \"this was harder than just throwing money and compute and optimization at it\". And that will be the new measure of what is a hard problem.",

      "author_id": "UCogL5HZ08r3GHokKFussW9A",

      "id": "UgxJ3CyOhl9UZU9wniR4AaABAg",
      "parent": "root",
      "text": "I suspect there will be no more than a few million humanoid robots. Once we get these robots and software using AGI… then we will realize that the VAST majority of what people do all day is useless or actually destructive. Our current economy runs on paychecks not actually being productive or producing value. Monetary value does not equal objective value which resides with promulgating healthy bodies and environments. As soon as AGI makes human labor obsolete we will stop doing so much to begin with, labor will be redomesticated to the individual, home, local environment. Growing your own food, solar panels, making your own tools, educating yourself via AGI and robust browsing interfaces. What are they gonna sit in offices, no! Are they gonna work in factories? No, it will just be automated assembly lines largely. Will they work at cafes, handing out coffee??? I think the era of mass labor was based on the need for paychecks, as was the old social contract, in the future we will try to limit labor… because it’s more efficient and effective and enjoyable.",

      "text": " @daPawlak  they are completely detached from the reality of blue collar trades, there's no way their clunky robots will automate any of these jobs unless these industries shift to more modularity to accommodate them, even then it's far from obvious it will make economic sense for most companies. I think robotics will have some applications but all the jobs that require a high level of dexterity and improvisation will be safe for a long time",

      "author": "@M3t4M0rph-P.I",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/-SEFr1-OoOPHCVoI9DQToLoW1TqRlhIFVuQXTpb_jdQ1lUOpwD7bXzWB5vc93mln5ug4dKonQw=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

      "parent": "UgxWeynlOEPwp-J6uSV4AaABAg.AMzD49x8um1AMzr4cWxaLH",
      "text": "​ @M3t4M0rph-P.I  yeah robotics already do have impact. Like we have welding robots but we have human welders too. \nThe scifi android doing everything is silly but in general automation is ongoing and not going to stop.",

      "author_id": "UCMGBvUO_mo8I12ho5GKxmmg",
      "author": "@daPawlak",

      "parent": "UgxWeynlOEPwp-J6uSV4AaABAg.AMzD49x8um1AMzr4cWxaLH",
      "text": " @daPawlak  you're right, many industries have been using high tech assembly robots for some time. I was more thinking of the usual plumbing example because I've worked in construction. \nThe tech to 3D print concrete is already there and viable but everything else has to be done manually. \nMaybe in 15 years we get to fully viable automation for the rest of the building (electricity, plumbing, windows + doors and finishes). \nThat means in 30+ years we'll see these techniques widely adopted worldwide. \nThat's still a scary trend because in the end only renovation/maintenance/oversight jobs will remain.\nSo the hope is the robots will do crap work we'll have to constantly fix ;) Joking but things could easily turn out that way...",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UC_0YFPmK_hSvxMZlg26ZCmw",
      "author": "@M3t4M0rph-P.I",

      "text": "EXACTLY my thoughts… can’t really trust anything he says on estimates",

      "author": "@ChipWhitehouseTV",
      "author_thumbnail": "https://yt3.ggpht.com/b3tXp1G3DqWStP8tKYJhWKnYvrSMNgnkbsE6mC_vhZ_u1vc8PQ7U6TAucwSSqAXhuC6GzcBi=s88-c-k-c0x00ffffff-no-rj",

    {
      "id": "Ugy50gldCFdchZOcCL54AaABAg.AMz-oqzgv9YAN1-tGo0svb",
      "parent": "Ugy50gldCFdchZOcCL54AaABAg",
      "text": "You are vastly out of the ball park, physical AI models have been well on the road to recursive self improvement. Examples of models that have significantly reduced iteration time to new skills acquisition include: \n\nNvidia Groot R1 & Cosmos models \n\nFigure Robotics Helix model (which I suspect is built on top of it inspired by Nvidia's model as Nvidia is an investor)\n\nUnitree Robotics, Yes, so far they've shown off complex acrobatics and dancing, but clearly consistently improved the ability of the robot over time... Generality of function is just a matter of iterating the hardware and the model parameter sizes in lockstep. New abilities will simply emerge just as they have in the text domain. \n\nTesla FSD, many in the analyst space leave out this one of the first practical applications of a world model. Designed as such from the beginning... Running on custom inferencing silicon that is optimized for processing video... FSD has continued to develop extremely complex understanding of traffic scenarios, making it by far the most general autonomous driving AI in the world. Parameter sizes of the model continues to grow and it continues to increase its capabilities. It's currently operating as robo taxes in Austin and San Francisco and rapidly scaling. \n\nFSD, the same AI but trained within the embodiment of a physical body is what drives the Optimus robot, which is also scaling generality very quickly. \n\nBoston Dynamics Atlas 01, Boston Dynamics realized that the exquisite brittle complexity of the old method of robotic development based on heuristic code would not scale, so they went and quickly implemented a neural model and harnessed it to a new physical body based on an electric drivetrain as opposed to the hydraulics of the original Atlas and what they presented has been astounding. \n\n\nThat's just a short list of the top of my head, there are dozens more and many of them are utilizing the Nvidia stack for hardware and software training, as well as utilizing the nvidia-based base models for Groot and Cosmos to tighten the iteration loop for generality.... Again, we're already in the place where we're rapidly approaching where cursive self-improvement the human is still in the middle in the form of facilitating the training process and the deployment to inferencing. That is a solvable problem for the future, but the ability to derive significant commercial impact using the current method is the same as it is in robotics as it has been the development of the llm and that has been extremely lucrative for the hyperscalers.",
      "like_count": 0,
      "author_id": "UCRASbNkgqK1wKYFDXlyc1yg",

      "text": " @Dannyboi91 the big bottleneck is transfer movements. Robots operated a ton of manufacturing tasks but they could not unload or load parts. ## Description

Sergey Levine is one of the world’s top robotics researchers and co-founder of Physical Intelligence. He thinks we’re on the cusp of a “self-improvement flywheel” for general-purpose robots. His median estimate for when robots will be able to run households entirely autonomously? 2030.

If Sergey’s right, the world 5 years from now will be an *insanely* different place than it is today. This conversation focuses on understanding how we get there: we dive into foundation models for robotics, and how we scale both the data and the hardware necessary to enable a full-blown robotics explosion.

The key here is prior knowledge.&nbsp; In order to effectively learn from your own&nbsp; experience, it turns out that it's really,&nbsp;&nbsp; really important to already know&nbsp; something about what you're doing.&nbsp;

Otherwise it takes far too long, just like&nbsp; it takes a person, when they're a child,&nbsp;&nbsp; a very long time to learn very basic things, to&nbsp; learn to write for the first time, for example.&nbsp; Once you already have some knowledge, then&nbsp;

you can learn new things very quickly.&nbsp; The purpose of training the models with supervised&nbsp; learning now is to build out that foundation that&nbsp;&nbsp; provides the prior knowledge so they can&nbsp; figure things out much more quickly later.&nbsp;

It's a little circular, of course,&nbsp;&nbsp; and as with all circular things, you have to&nbsp; bootstrap it and try to get that engine going.&nbsp; But it seems like it is an easier&nbsp; problem to address than, for example,&nbsp;&nbsp;

the problem of digital devices. Work goes into creating computers,&nbsp;&nbsp; phones, et cetera. But the computers and&nbsp;&nbsp; phones don't themselves help with the work.

Right. I guess feedback loops go both ways.&nbsp; They can help you or they can help&nbsp; others and it's a positive sum world.&nbsp; It's not necessarily bad that they help others. But to the extent that a lot of the things&nbsp;&nbsp;

which would go into this feedback loop—the&nbsp; sub-component, manufacturing and supply chain,&nbsp;&nbsp; already exist in China—it seems like the&nbsp; stronger feedback loop would exist in China.&nbsp;&nbsp; Then there's a separate discussion.&nbsp;

Maybe that's fine, maybe that's good,&nbsp;&nbsp; and maybe they'll continue exporting this to us. But I just find it notable that whenever I talk&nbsp;&nbsp; to guests about different things, it's&nbsp; just like, "Yeah, within a few years the&nbsp;&nbsp;

key bottleneck to every single part of&nbsp; the supply chain here will be something&nbsp;&nbsp; that China is the 80% world supplier of." This is why I said before that something&nbsp;&nbsp; really important to get right here&nbsp;

is a balanced robotics ecosystem.&nbsp; AI is tremendously exciting, but we should&nbsp; also recognize that getting AI right is&nbsp;&nbsp; not the only thing that we need to do. We need to think about how to balance our&nbsp;&nbsp;

priorities, our investment, the kind&nbsp; of things that we spend our time on.&nbsp; Just as an example, at Physical Intelligence&nbsp; we do take hardware very seriously.&nbsp; We build a lot of our own things and we want to&nbsp;

have a hardware roadmap alongside our AI roadmap.&nbsp;&nbsp; But that's just us. For the United States,&nbsp; arguably for human civilization as a whole,&nbsp;&nbsp; we need to think about these&nbsp; problems very holistically.&nbsp;

It is easy to get distracted sometimes&nbsp; when there's a lot of excitement,&nbsp;&nbsp; a lot of progress in one area like AI. We are tempted to lose track of other things,&nbsp;&nbsp; including things you've said. There's a hardware&nbsp;

component. There's an infrastructure component&nbsp;&nbsp; with compute and things like that. In general it's good to have a more&nbsp;&nbsp; holistic view of these things. I wish we had more holistic&nbsp;&nbsp;

conversations about that sometimes. From the perspective of society as a whole,&nbsp;&nbsp; how should they be thinking about the&nbsp; advances in robotics and knowledge work?&nbsp; Basically society should be&nbsp;

planning for full automation.&nbsp; There will be a period in which people's work&nbsp; is way more valuable because there's this huge&nbsp;&nbsp; boom in the economy where we’re building&nbsp; all these data centers and factories.&nbsp;

Eventually humans can do things with their&nbsp; body and we can do things with our mind.&nbsp; There's not some secret third thing. What should society be planning for?&nbsp; It should be full automation of humans.

Society will also be much wealthier.&nbsp; Presumably there are ways to do this such that&nbsp; everybody is much better off than they are today.&nbsp; But the end state, the light at the end of the&nbsp; tunnel, is the full automation but plus super&nbsp;&nbsp;

wealthy society with some redistribution&nbsp; or whatever way to figure that out.&nbsp; I don't know if you disagree&nbsp; with that characterization.&nbsp; At some level that's a very&nbsp;

reasonable way to look at things.&nbsp; But if there's one thing that I've learned&nbsp; about technology, it's that it rarely&nbsp;&nbsp; evolves quite the way that people expect. Sometimes the journey is just as important&nbsp;&nbsp;

as the destination. It's very difficult&nbsp;&nbsp; to plan ahead for an end state. Directionally, what you said makes a lot of sense.&nbsp; I do think that it's very important for us&nbsp;

collectively to think about how to structure&nbsp;&nbsp; the world around us in a way that is amenable to&nbsp; greater and greater automation across all sectors.&nbsp; But we should really think about the journey&nbsp; just as much as the destination, because&nbsp;&nbsp;

things evolve in all sorts of unpredictable ways. We'll find automation showing up in all sorts of&nbsp;&nbsp; places, probably not the places we expect first. The constant here that is really important&nbsp;&nbsp; is that education is really, really valuable.

Education is the best buffer somebody has&nbsp;&nbsp; against the negative effects of change. If there is one single lever that we can pull&nbsp;&nbsp; collectively as a society, it's more education. Is that true? Moravec's paradox is that the&nbsp;&nbsp;

things which are most beneficial from education&nbsp; for humans might be the easiest to automate&nbsp;&nbsp; because it's really easy to educate AIs. You can throw the textbooks that would take&nbsp;&nbsp; you eight years of grad school&nbsp;

to do at them in an afternoon.&nbsp; What education gives you is flexibility. It's less about the particular facts you&nbsp;&nbsp; know, as it is about your ability to&nbsp; acquire skills, acquire understanding.&nbsp;

It has to be a good education. Yeah. Okay, Sergey, thank you so much&nbsp;&nbsp; for coming on the podcast. Super fascinating. Yeah, this was intense. Tough questions.

> The brain is more like having many CPUs/threads operating at the same time on different values, rather than a GPU that has to take a static matrix of values one at a time. The brains neurones are unconstrained in their parallelism. > 🎯 Key points for quick navigation:
> 
> 00:28 🤖 Physical Intelligence is focused on creating general-purpose robotic foundation models for versatile task performance.
> 01:29 🧺 Current robots can perform basic tasks like folding laundry, but this is just the beginning of their capabilities.
> 02:55 🗣️ Future robots should autonomously manage complex household tasks based on simple prompts and adapt over time.
> 03:52 📈 Successful robots will require common sense, continuous learning, and the ability to handle edge cases intelligently.
> 04:45 🔄 Once robots demonstrate basic competence, they can be deployed to learn and improve from real-world experience.
> 05:40 ⏳ Expect robots to be useful in single-digit years, potentially within one to two years for basic tasks.
> 07:25 🤝 Human supervision will help robots improve quickly through collaborative learning from both actions and verbal instructions.
> 09:28 🛠️ The scope of robotic capabilities will gradually expand as they gain more skills, similar to the evolution of coding assistants.
> 10:50 💼 In five years, robots may handle most blue-collar work, but this will depend on the scope of tasks they can perform.
> 13:00 🚀 Gradual integration of robots in a human-in-the-loop setup will enhance their effectiveness and productivity.
> 18:34 ⚙️ Advances in perception technology have improved robotics since the early days of self-driving cars, leading to better capabilities today.
> 21:00 🧠 The combination of common sense and the ability to learn from mistakes will help robots tackle complex tasks effectively.
> 22:48 🚀 Robotic foundation models require not only fundamental research but also significant industrial-scale efforts to be effective.
> 23:18 📊 Achieving practical capabilities in robots involves collecting representative data at scale and ensuring a singular focus on foundational models.
> 24:17 🧩 Scaling capabilities requires understanding which factors contribute to performance, including robustness and efficiency in real-world tasks.
> 26:19 🔄 The key is not how much data is needed to complete robotics but how much is required to initiate a self-sustaining data collection cycle.
> 27:46 🧠 The π0 model combines vision-language elements with motor control, optimizing decision-making and action execution for robots.
> 30:32 🥅 Recent AI innovations enhance robotics by allowing models to leverage prior knowledge, improving task execution through learned abstractions.
> 32:35 🔄 Differences in how text and visual data are represented can hinder transfer learning between modalities, affecting generative model performance.

> Also strange to give that as an example of compositional generalization. If you have a dictionary with English and IPA spellings, then you literally have a lookup table in the training data. Compositional generalization would be if you had half a dictionary, and it figures out the other half, by inferring English pronunciation rules (as far as there are such rules) and how to compose them (for example if it had seen the example knife-knives and the IPA spellings, and inferred how wife-wives should be pronounced. But it might get confused by life-lives, since there are two pronunciations of lives).
> 
> There is evidence that Transformers can learn compositional generalization, but it looks like it requires a different kind of learning task then the next-token predictions that LLMs are mainly trained to do (see "Human-like systematic generalization through a meta-learning neural network" )

> I'll offer a little personal experience. I'm a fairly serious hobbyist in the AI/RL and robotics space. A few weeks ago I wrapped up a course that included a small mobile robot with SLAM(think basic autonomous navigation) in a simulator. I'm three weeks into making that same functionality work in a "mirrored" physical robot and it's not the hardest thing I've ever worked on, but there have been some pretty significant challenges..and that's an identical robot going from sim to real. 
> 
> I can also say that training models for RL tasks tends to require you to know your outputs/inputs ahead of time, and even small changes can throw things off. Something trained to play chess from one side won't understand intuitively how to play from the other side like a human would. That's something you have to think about ahead of time and build into your training, or sanitize your inputs for consistency. 
> 
> So, if we combine those things, I can say that applying any kind of software to the physical world is going to have hurdles, and applying a robotics AI model to something it wasn't designed for is going to be difficult. Difficult isn't the same thing as impossible though. I can see a world where we standardize on enough inputs/outputs across various bots to use shared models, assuming they allow heavy configuration. 
> 
> What I suspect we'll see more of in the near future is limited models integrated for common functionality. Maybe your robot follows a traditional algorithm to drive to the kitchen, but one model is connected to a ChatGPT API, to recognize that you asked for breakfast, and another robot arm model takes over to open the fridge and start cooking eggs. 
> 
> 
> Just my 2c.

> 12:04 You can't just use the revenue of the AI companies to determine the value LLMs are producing in the economy, because the individuals and companies that are using the LLMs are receiving value from them which is generating money (and saving money) for them, which is separate from the revenue of the AI companies themselves. For example, if a company buys access to an LLM for $1000 per year, and that allows a 10 person team to become a 5 person team by using it, and the 5 people that were let go were making $100K per year each, that resulted in the company effectively profiting $499K despite only paying $1000 for the LLM. All that value generated in the economy goes unreported if you're only looking at the $1000 payment to the AI company. On top of that there is also the value generated by the LLM's work output, for example if it's used to create a product that sells for $1M, now the company profited $1.499M just from that $1000 payment to the AI company. So in summary there's not a 1-1 ratio for the AI companys' revenue to the value LLMs are producing in the economy. Similarly to how you can't just look at an employee's paycheck to determine the value that employee generated in the economy.

> 
> Nvidia Groot R1 & Cosmos models 
> 
> Figure Robotics Helix model (which I suspect is built on top of it inspired by Nvidia's model as Nvidia is an investor)
> 
> Unitree Robotics, Yes, so far they've shown off complex acrobatics and dancing, but clearly consistently improved the ability of the robot over time... Generality of function is just a matter of iterating the hardware and the model parameter sizes in lockstep. New abilities will simply emerge just as they have in the text domain. 
> 
> Tesla FSD, many in the analyst space leave out this one of the first practical applications of a world model. Designed as such from the beginning... Running on custom inferencing silicon that is optimized for processing video... FSD has continued to develop extremely complex understanding of traffic scenarios, making it by far the most general autonomous driving AI in the world. Parameter sizes of the model continues to grow and it continues to increase its capabilities. It's currently operating as robo taxes in Austin and San Francisco and rapidly scaling. 
> 
> FSD, the same AI but trained within the embodiment of a physical body is what drives the Optimus robot, which is also scaling generality very quickly. 
> 
> Boston Dynamics Atlas 01, Boston Dynamics realized that the exquisite brittle complexity of the old method of robotic development based on heuristic code would not scale, so they went and quickly implemented a neural model and harnessed it to a new physical body based on an electric drivetrain as opposed to the hydraulics of the original Atlas and what they presented has been astounding. 
> 
> 
> That's just a short list of the top of my head, there are dozens more and many of them are utilizing the Nvidia stack for hardware and software training, as well as utilizing the nvidia-based base models for Groot and Cosmos to tighten the iteration loop for generality.... Again, we're already in the place where we're rapidly approaching where cursive self-improvement the human is still in the middle in the form of facilitating the training process and the deployment to inferencing. That is a solvable problem for the future, but the ability to derive significant commercial impact using the current method is the same as it is in robotics as it has been the development of the llm and that has been extremely lucrative for the hyperscalers.
